pairs.source_text: et visus idoneus maternae necis patrator Anicetus, classi apud Misenum, ut memoravi, praefectus
pairs.question: Quem Tacitus necis Agrippinae, matris Neronis, patratorem fuisse tradit, classi apud Misenum praefectum?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Tacitus report to have been the agent of the murder of Agrippina, Nero's mother, the prefect of the fleet at Misenum?
pairs.derivation: The murder of Nero's mother Agrippina. Anchored to Agrippina (Nero's mother) + the fleet prefecture at Misenum; single named person, supported verbatim by 'maternae necis patrator Anicetus, classi apud Misenum ... praefectus' (maternae necis = the murder of Nero's mother, i.e. Agrippina, the subject throughout 14.1-9). Indirect statement (Anicetum ... patratorem fuisse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: Anicetus the freedman as the agent of Agrippina's killing is a stock fact of Nero's reign.

pairs.source_text: quando Quinquatruum festos dies apud Baias frequentabat. illuc matrem elicit, ferendas parentium iracundias et placandum animum dictitans
pairs.question: Quo Nero matrem suam Agrippinam, per Quinquatruum festos dies, dolo elicuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To what place did Nero lure his mother Agrippina by a trick during the festival days of the Quinquatrus, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero + his mother Agrippina + the Quinquatrus festival; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Quinquatruum festos dies apud Baias frequentabat. illuc matrem elicit' (matrem = Agrippina). Direct question (Quo ... elicuit) mirroring the source's 'illuc'. Closed-book: Nero luring Agrippina to Baiae to stage the shipwreck is a famous episode.

pairs.source_text: obtulit ingenium Anicetus libertus, classi apud Misenum praefectus et pueritiae Neronis educator ac mutuis odiis Agrippinae invisus. ergo navem posse componi docet, cuius pars ipso in mari per artem soluta effunderet ignaram
pairs.question: Quo dolo Anicetus Agrippinam, Neronis matrem, primum interfici posse docuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.answer: Nave quae in mari per artem solveretur.
pairs.question_en: By what trick did Anicetus teach that Agrippina, Nero's mother, could first be killed, according to Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: By a ship contrived to come apart at sea.
pairs.derivation: The collapsing-ship plot against Agrippina. Anchored to Anicetus + Agrippina; the means is supported verbatim by 'navem posse componi docet, cuius pars ipso in mari per artem soluta effunderet ignaram'. Indirect statement (interfici posse) governed by docuit; answer is a relative clause with characteristic subjunctive. Closed-book: the self-dismantling ship off Baiae is the signature detail of the Agrippina murder.

pairs.source_text: Rex Icenorum Prasutagus, longa opulentia clarus, Caesarem heredem duasque filias scripserat, tali obsequio ratus regnumque et domum suam procul iniuria fore.
pairs.question: Quis rex Icenorum, Caesarem et duas filias suas heredes scribens, apud Tacitum memoratur?
pairs.question_en: Which king of the Iceni, naming Caesar and his two daughters as heirs, is mentioned in Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Iceni + the bequest naming Caesar (Nero) and the king's two daughters as heirs; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Rex Icenorum Prasutagus ... Caesarem heredem duasque filias scripserat'. Direct question, indicative memoratur. Closed-book: Prasutagus, king of the Iceni and husband of Boudicca, is a standard fact of the British revolt.

pairs.source_text: iam primum uxor eius Boudicca verberibus adfecta et filiae stupro violatae sunt
pairs.question: Quae fuit uxor Prasutagi, regis Icenorum, quae verberibus adfecta postea Romanis rebellavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the wife of Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, who after being flogged then rebelled against the Romans, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Prasutagus king of the Iceni; single named person, supported verbatim by 'uxor eius Boudicca verberibus adfecta' (eius = Prasutagus, just named in 14.31). Her leadership of the revolt follows at 14.35 ('Boudicca curru filias prae se vehens'). Direct question, indicative rebellavit. Closed-book: Boudicca, queen of the Iceni, leader of the revolt against Rome, is among the most famous figures of Roman Britain.

pairs.question: Quo genere mortis Boudicca, Britannorum dux, vitam finivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: By what kind of death did Boudicca, the leader of the Britons, end her life, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Boudicca + the manner of her death; single short answer, supported verbatim by 'Boudicca vitam veneno finivit'. Direct question, indicative finivit. Closed-book: that Boudicca took poison after her defeat is the standard Tacitean account of her end.

pairs.source_text: sed tum Paulinus Suetonius obtinebat Britannos, scientia militiae et rumore populi
pairs.question: Quis dux Romanus, eo tempore quo Boudicca rebellavit, Britanniam obtinebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which Roman commander was governing Britain at the time Boudicca rebelled, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Britain + the time of Boudicca's revolt; single named person, supported verbatim by 'tum Paulinus Suetonius obtinebat Britannos'. He defeats Boudicca at 14.37. Direct question, indicative obtinebat. Closed-book: Suetonius Paulinus as the governor who crushed the British revolt is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: igitur Monam insulam, incolis validam et receptaculum perfugarum, adgredi parat, navesque fabricatur plano alveo adversus breve et incertum.
pairs.question: Quam insulam, Druidarum sedem, Suetonius Paulinus, dux Romanus in Britannia, oppugnare paravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which island, the seat of the Druids, did Suetonius Paulinus, the Roman commander in Britain, prepare to attack, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Suetonius Paulinus + the Druids; single named place, supported verbatim by 'Monam insulam ... adgredi parat'. The Druids and their sacred groves on Mona are described in the next chapter (14.30: 'Druidaeque circum ... excisique luci'). Direct question, indicative paravit. Closed-book: Suetonius's assault on the druidic stronghold of Mona is a well-known episode.

pairs.source_text: ad hoc templum divo Claudio constitutum quasi arx aeternae dominationibus adspiciebatur, delectique sacerdotes specie religionis omnes fortunas effundebant.
pairs.question: Cui divo apud Camulodunum templum constitutum erat, quod a Britannis quasi arx aeternae dominationis spectabatur, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To which deified emperor had a temple been established at Camulodunum, which the Britons regarded as a citadel of eternal domination, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the colony Camulodunum (named in the same chapter, 'in coloniam Camulodunum recens deducti'); single named person, supported verbatim by 'templum divo Claudio constitutum quasi arx aeternae dominationibus adspiciebatur'. Direct question, indicative constitutum erat. Closed-book: the temple of the deified Claudius at Camulodunum, a flashpoint of the revolt, is a documented fact.

pairs.source_text: ad septuaginta milia civium et sociorum iis, quae memoravi, locis cecidisse constitit.
pairs.question: Quot fere civium sociorumque milia in tribus oppidis a Britannis captis, Camuloduno, Londinio, Verulamio, cecidisse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: About how many thousands of citizens and allies does Tacitus report fell in the three towns captured by the Britons, Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the three towns sacked in the revolt (Camulodunum 14.31-32, Londinium and Verulamium 14.33 = the 'loci quae memoravi'); single number, supported verbatim by 'ad septuaginta milia civium et sociorum ... cecidisse constitit'. Direct question, indicative tradit. Closed-book: the ~70,000 dead in Boudicca's sack of the towns is the standard figure for the revolt's toll.

pairs.source_text: quippe sunt qui paulo minus quam octoginta milia Britannorum cecidisse tradant, militum quadringentis ferme interfectis nec multo amplius vulneratis.
pairs.question: In proelio quo Suetonius Paulinus Boudiccam vicit, quot fere milia Britannorum cecidisse traditur?
pairs.question_en: In the battle in which Suetonius Paulinus defeated Boudicca, about how many thousands of Britons are recorded to have fallen?
pairs.answer_en: A little less than eighty thousand.
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the decisive battle of Suetonius Paulinus against Boudicca; single number, supported verbatim by 'sunt qui paulo minus quam octoginta milia Britannorum cecidisse tradant'. The matching Roman loss (~400) appears in the same sentence. Impersonal traditur mirrors the source's 'sunt qui ... tradant'. Closed-book: the ~80,000 Britons fallen against ~400 Romans is the celebrated statistic of the battle.

pairs.source_text: exturbat Octaviam, sterilem dictitans; exim Poppaeae coniungitur.
pairs.question: Quam in matrimonium duxit Nero, postquam Octaviam, sterilem dictitans, repudiavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Nero marry after he divorced Octavia, calling her barren, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero + Octavia + the divorce; single named person, supported verbatim by 'exturbat Octaviam, sterilem dictitans; exim Poppaeae coniungitur'. Direct question, indicative duxit. Closed-book: Nero's divorce of Octavia and marriage to Poppaea Sabina is a stock fact of his reign.

pairs.source_text: eaque sibi comperta edicto memorat insulaque Pandateria Octaviam claudit.
pairs.question: In quam insulam Nero Octaviam, repudiatam coniugem, relegavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: To which island did Nero banish Octavia, his divorced wife, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero + Octavia (his divorced wife); single named place, supported verbatim by 'insulaque Pandateria Octaviam claudit'. Direct question, indicative relegavit. Closed-book: Octavia's banishment to Pandateria (and death there) is a documented fact of AD 62.

pairs.source_text: concessitque vita Burrus, incertum valetudine an veneno... quippe Caesar duos praetoriis cohortibus imposuerat, Faenium Rufum ex vulgi favore, quia rem frumentariam sine quaestu tractabat, Ofonium Tigellinum, veterem impudicitiam atque infamiam in eo secutus.
pairs.question: Quos duos viros Nero, mortuo Burro, praetoriis cohortibus praefecit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which two men did Nero put in charge of the praetorian cohorts after Burrus died, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the death of the praetorian prefect Burrus + the praetorian command; two named persons, supported verbatim by 'concessitque vita Burrus ... Caesar duos praetoriis cohortibus imposuerat, Faenium Rufum ... Ofonium Tigellinum'. Direct question, indicative praefecit. Closed-book: that Burrus's death led to the joint prefecture of Faenius Rufus and Tigellinus is a standard fact of Nero's later reign.
